doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Jim Cullum band style and the Riverwalk radio show
summary: The band's traditional but varied repertoire on NPR's Riverwalk, with guests like Jay McShann and Bob Wilber.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Jim Cullum is kind of dedicated to keeping alive a certain genre of music?

Yes and no. It’s definitely more of a traditional style that he goes for. But over the years that I was on the band we experimented and did a lot of different things. We never got into doing hardcore bop or anything like that. We moved into swing and mainstream quite a bit and did some of those kind of things. And we did that National Public Radio show that I was on for five years.

Riverwalk, yeah. And we got into many different styles of playing, depending on a lot of times we had different guest stars and stuff — like we were doing big band swing when Jay McShann was there, we were doing all of Hootie’s big hits, which was that period, and talking about Charlie Parker and so forth. So it just depended. And all the guys on the band are great musicians and fairly — can adapt to that style. I ended up having to play saxophone more on a lot of those things too, I was playing alto and so forth. Bob Wilber came in, he and I did a couple of duets on saxophone, soprano and alto, and that kind of thing. So it’s not really what Jim wants to keep the band doing, but on the same token, for that particular show you can’t just stay in one area you have to be able to expand some. Otherwise you’re going to lose the interest of the audience.
Right. I think Joe Williams appeared on that.
Yeah, that was later on. I’m very disappointed, I was gone by the time Joe appeared on the show and it would have been great.
